newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian parliament to meet, Berisha may resign.
newsitem.headline: Albanian parliament to meet, Berisha may resign.

text.p: Albania's new governing majority prepared for the first meeting of the new parliament on Wednesday and newspapers said President Sali Berisha was expected to hand in his promised resignation.
No comment was available from the presidency, and diplomats said they had no confirmation of his intentions.

Berisha has promised to step down once the new parliament is in place but his resignation has been eagerly awaited by his Socialist Party opponents, who feared he could try to influence the formation of the new cabinet.
"Today the former cardiologist will not be president any more. The new president has come," said the pro-Berisha Albania daily, referring to Socialist Party Secretary-General Rexhep Mejdani.

Describing Berisha as a prominent fighter for democracy, it said Mejdani, a 52-year-old physics professor, had no moral right to be president because he was allegedly backed by rebels and criminal gangs.
The Socialists say Berisha should resign the presidency in order to take a seat in parliament as a deputy for his Democratic Party.

Following constitutional court rulings on disputes and some changing of alliances, the Socialists and their coalition allies will have 118 seats in the 155-seat parliament, while the Democrats have 24.

The Democrats will boycott Wednesday's session, which starts at 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) to protest at the conduct of the poll, which was described by international monitors as acceptable, if far from perfect.

They complain the elections were held in a climate of terror and they were unable to campaign in the south, but diplomats say their losses even in Tirana put paid to any serious claims of manipulation.
"The era of Kalashnikovs starts. Clocks in Albania have gone back six years. Today, the parliament of the gangs," said Rilindja Demokratike.
Berisha's government resigned in March at the height of unrest in which more than 1,500 people have been killed.
The first tasks facing the new assembly will be to restore law and order and to resolve the economic chaos left by the collapse of high-interest investment schemes.

"June 29 elections were the only chance to put an end to one of the gloomiest periods in the history of the Albanian people," said the Socialist daily Zeri i Popullit, promising the new parliament would play a leading role in a new, more hopeful era for the country.

Albania's first non-communist president, Berisha was initially praised in the West for rapid introduction of market reforms, but enthusiasm faded as he resorted to increasingly authoritarian methods and failed to check the spread of the pyramid schemes.
The European Union in a statement on Tuesday urged Albania's political factions to do everything necessary to allow a new government with a popular mandate to be set up.

Armouries were looted at the start of the unrest and the security situation is becoming more precarious with the gradual withdrawal of international peacekeepers who deployed in April to assure security for the elections and guard aid deliveries. All the 7,000 troops are expected to be gone by mid-August.

Residents of the southern port of Vlore reported heavy fighting on Monday night, while an explosion wrecked two cafes in Tirana early on Tuesday and army sources said thieves had stolen missiles thought to be Chinese-made Silkworms from a depot near the Greek border.

Democracy has shaky foundations in Albania, where Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha ruled with an iron fist for 40 years until his death in April 1985, crushing opposition and isolating his state under a policy of self-reliance.

His successor, communist President Ramiz Alia, ruled out change, but a wave of anti-government demonstrations from July 1990 gradually led to reforms, culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
